overview: This sortie is about understanding what the hydraulic system buys you before you go spin, OCF, and crosswind work. Be ready to brief the hydraulic system well enough to explain normal versus emergency services, then keep the spin, OCF, anti-spin, and crosswind boundaries straight once the aircraft departs normal flight.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full hydraulic walk-through. For this event, know what hydraulic power you are counting on in normal flight, what changes when the normal system is lost, and which indications change your gear, flap, or NWS decisions.

children.text: Normal hydraulic power runs the landing gear, TO/LDG flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
The engine-driven pump maintains roughly 3000 +/- 120 PSI from a 5-quart reservoir. That normal-system pressure is what you are relying on anytime you move gear, flaps, or speed brake.
Think normal versus emergency: the power package and selector manifold do the routine work, and the emergency accumulator gives you one backup shot if the main system is gone.
HYDR FL LO points you toward a fluid-quantity, leak, or normal-system problem and should make you stop assuming normal gear or flap operation is guaranteed.
EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO suggests a leak or hydraulic-fuse problem and a thinner backup margin.
Emergency gear extension leaves the inboard doors extended, and emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector but the flaps cannot be retracted once they are out.
Disengage NWS before sharp turns that require differential braking.
Do not take off with a known NWS problem; centering issues can create takeoff or landing control problems.
If the emergency accumulator has been discharged for maintenance, the related caution should be out before flight.

items.text: The spin is not a finesse maneuver. It is a deliberate stalled-yaw entry used to teach recognition, orientation, and disciplined recovery once the aircraft departs normal flight.

children.text: Trim the aircraft in slow cruise at 150 KIAS.
Minimum entry altitude is 13,500 feet AGL. Enter below 22,000 feet pressure altitude and recover before 10,000 feet pressure altitude.
The entry is built to begin with PCL going to IDLE before the nose comes up; do not build the pitch picture first and pull power late.
Perform the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist and clear the area thoroughly, including TCAS as appropriate.
Check wings level, retard PCL to IDLE, and smoothly raise the nose to about 30 degrees above the horizon.
At the stick shaker, lead the stall with slight rudder in the desired spin direction.
When the aircraft stalls and the nose pitches down, smoothly apply full rudder in the direction of spin and full back stick with ailerons neutral.
Call out altitude, AOA, airspeed, and turn-needle direction so the phase of the spin stays clear.
The maneuver is complete when the IP-directed recovery is finished, oil pressure is checked and reported normal, and the aircraft is back in controlled flight inside the working area.
Raising the nose before PCL is fully at IDLE.
Letting disorientation delay recognition or recovery.
Failing to neutralize controls as rotation stops or pulling too aggressively into a secondary stall.
Spins are flown clean. If gear or flaps are down in an unintentional spin, get them up immediately to avoid airspeed-limit damage.
Ailerons remain neutral throughout intentional spin training.
Silence the gear-warning horn before entry so it does not interfere with recognition calls.

items.text: OCF recovery procedures are for post-stall gyrations and incipient spins where the aircraft has departed normal flight but has not yet stabilized into a true steady-state spin.

children.text: Post-stall gyration shows up as uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high or stalled AOA, and controls that feel ineffective or wrong.
An incipient spin shows stalled AOA, a fully deflected turn needle, and airspeed changing toward the steady-state value. Expect about the first two turns here.
If you are not yet in a stabilized 120-135 KIAS, 18+ units AOA, steady-state picture, stay with OCF recovery rather than jumping to anti-spin inputs.
PCL - IDLE.
CONTROLS - NEUTRAL, physically not just trimmed neutral.
ALTITUDE - CHECK.
RECOVER FROM UNUSUAL ATTITUDE once the stall breaks and the aircraft begins responding normally.
If the aircraft is not recovering as expected, it is common for the elevator to still be slightly aft of neutral; feed in forward stick only enough to find true neutral.
Do not start inventing anti-spin inputs early just because the motion feels dramatic.
If the aircraft is in an unrecoverable descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Anti-spin recovery procedures are for a true steady-state spin, not for every out-of-control motion. The key is recognizing when neutral-controls recovery is no longer the right answer.

children.text: A steady-state erect spin is identified by 18+ units AOA, airspeed stabilized around 120-135 KIAS, and the turn needle fully deflected in the direction of spin.
At that point the spin has stabilized enough that anti-spin controls, not neutral controls, are required.
Apply full rudder opposite the turn-needle direction.
Immediately follow with smooth, positive forward stick to a position forward of neutral.
Keep ailerons neutral and hold the controls until rotation stops.
Then neutralize the controls, level the wings by horizon reference, make a smooth pullout, check oil pressure, and add power as required.
Progressive and aggravated spins are not handled by random experimentation; if the motion has not stabilized into a true steady-state picture, default back to OCF recovery logic.

Intentional inverted departures and inverted spins are prohibited. If an inverted-spin picture develops, the recovery inputs differ from erect-spin recovery and the aircraft requires post-flight scrutiny.
Power-on or inverted departures/spins place very high loads on the engine and propeller system and may produce low oil pressure or CHIP indications.
A spiral can look like a spin, but anti-spin inputs will not stop a spiral and may worsen it.
Do not hold full aft stick turn after turn waiting for the airplane to save you. Once the spin is clearly steady-state, transition to the proper anti-spin inputs.
Forward stick well beyond neutral can create oil-pressure issues and engine damage, and anti-spin logic should never replace proper phase recognition.

items.text: This event expects you to apply crosswind technique repeatedly, not just once. The student value is showing that the crosswind picture survives takeoff, touch-and-go, and full-stop landing without drifting back into late or sloppy corrections.

children.text: Use up to full aileron into the wind at the start of the takeoff roll, relax it as speed builds, and use rudder to stop weather-vaning.
Rotate firmly at flying speed to avoid skipping, then level the wings and let the aircraft crab into the wind once safely airborne.
On downwind and in the final turn, adjust bank and power for overshooting or undershooting winds and do not exceed 45 degrees of bank to make final.
Use the wing-low method on final: aileron into the wind to stop drift, rudder to align the nose with the runway, and extra power as required to offset cross-control drag.
During gusty conditions, add half the gust factor to final approach speed, up to 10 knots.
Do not level the wings in the flare. Land on the upwind main first with zero side motion.
On full stops, keep increasing aileron into the wind as the aircraft slows and the controls lose effectiveness.
On touch-and-goes, hold the crosswind controls on the deck, use positive rotation, then level the wings and allow the aircraft to crab into the wind after liftoff.
If you cannot prevent overshooting final without exceeding 45 degrees of bank, or if drift/crab is not under control before touchdown, wave off.
Skipping on takeoff, landing in a crab, and letting the upwind wing rise on rollout all come from losing the wind-correction picture as the aircraft slows or lifts off.
Do not aggressively yank the aircraft back to centerline after an off-center touchdown. Keep the wing under control first.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the boundaries straight: know what hydraulics powers, fly the spin entry cleanly, use neutral-controls OCF recovery until a true steady-state spin exists, and keep crosswind corrections alive all the way through touchdown.

summary: Hydraulic-system essentials, spin recognition, OCF versus anti-spin recovery, and repeated crosswind pattern application.

items.text: Start with purpose, then explain how normal hydraulic pressure is created and routed, then finish with what the emergency system does when the main system is gone. That sequence is much easier to brief than listing parts at random.

children.text: Purpose: provide hydraulic power for landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
Normal-system flow: power package creates pressure, selector manifold routes it to the commanded service.
Emergency-system flow: accumulator pressure is saved for one-time emergency landing-gear and flap use.

items.text: The power package is the pressure-producing heart of the hydraulic system. It houses the reservoir, pump, and the components that regulate and protect system pressure.

children.text: The reservoir holds 5 quarts of hydraulic fluid, and the engine-driven pump maintains about 3000 +/- 120 PSI for the normal system.
A pressure reducer piston helps bring return pressure down, and the relief valve protects the system from overpressurization.
The pressure transmitter is what feeds the cockpit indication logic, and the filters are there to keep contamination from becoming a hydraulic problem.
The slide-valve assembly keeps the emergency system isolated during normal operations so the accumulator stays available for when you actually need it.
Think of 1800 PSI as the rough floor where the system still has enough pressure to do useful work, even though the normal target is much closer to 3000 PSI.

items.text: The selector manifold is the traffic cop. It takes pressure from the power package and sends it to the system you actually command from the cockpit.

children.text: Landing gear: the gear selector valve routes pressure to the main gear, nose gear, and inboard-door actuators. Three green lights mean down and locked; no lights mean up; a red light means transit or an associated gear-door condition.
Flaps: separate TO and LDG selector-valve paths let the flap actuator move the torque tube and flap system to the commanded setting.
Speed brake: hydraulic pressure extends it, and it auto-retracts with PCL to MAX, flap selection to LDG, or manual retract selection.
Nosewheel steering is hydraulically powered and gives about 12 degrees left or right of castor when engaged.
NWS is for ground steering only. If you need a sharper turn, disengage NWS before using differential braking so you are not fighting or damaging the steering system.
A speed brake that droops on the ramp is not automatically a malfunction; with pressure removed, the brake can settle because hydraulic pressure normally holds it up.

items.text: The emergency system is built around a helium-precharged accumulator that stores pressure for one-time emergency extension of the landing gear and flaps.

children.text: Pulling the emergency gear-extension handle releases accumulator pressure, isolates the main system, and ports pressure to the landing-gear and inboard-door actuators.
After emergency gear extension, the inboard doors remain extended. That is normal for the emergency configuration.
Emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector, but it is powered through the emergency path and the flaps cannot be retracted once extended.
A hydraulic fuse helps limit fluid loss into the emergency system if a leak develops.
An EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO is the combination that should make you think leak or fuse trouble instead of normal accumulator depletion.
If the emergency accumulator was discharged for maintenance, make sure the caution has cleared before flight so you do not launch with the backup already spent.

items.text: Most weak hydraulic briefs come from forgetting to tie indications back to what service you will actually lose next.

children.text: HYDR FL LO is a normal-system cue. EHYD PX LO is an emergency-system cue. Seeing both together means more than seeing either one alone.
Do not brief NWS as an isolated taxi feature; in this event it matters because a steering problem can become a takeoff, landing, or crosswind-control problem.
Be explicit that the emergency system is one-time use. Students often remember it exists but forget that you are spending stored pressure, not switching to a second normal system.

title: Hydraulics, Spins, and Crosswinds
